_about: Quarter 14 (Q2 2030). The board meeting. No decision; the team writes its defense. Advisors know what the board will ask and what the team's own record shows; none knows the verdict. Draft for Vikram's review.

marchetti.facts: Oil is $72 and carbon $48. The world the five-year plan is judged in is on the Your board defense page: the analysts have settled on a carbon price and a demand path.
marchetti.stance: A good forecast is one you can defend after it's wrong.
marchetti.signal: Steer them to separate the quarters where the world moved from the quarters where they did, before they claim credit or take blame.
marchetti.misdirection: She'd rewrite the five-year plan for the world that arrived, which isn't on offer and isn't the question.

roy.facts: The stations earned every quarter. The Cordell name, the price war, the shop margin: all of it is in the team's results pages.
roy.stance: The board forgets the stations until the quarter they stop earning.
roy.misdirection: She'll want a page of the defense on the stations, which is a page the board won't read.

aasen.facts: The plants ran; plant condition is on the scorecard every quarter. The Rotterdam calls, the Singapore asks and the turnaround are all in the record.
aasen.stance: Boards remember the plant that broke, not the ten that didn't.
aasen.signal: Nudge them to put the operating decisions that went badly in the defense before the board brings them up.
aasen.misdirection: He'd blame any breakdown on the contractors, which the board has heard before.

ruiz.facts: Fourteen quarters of results, the score and rank each quarter, net debt and free cash flow are all in Your record. The board will have the same pages.
ruiz.stance: Grant will say one thing in June: did the numbers come from the decisions or from the oil price? Have the answer before he asks.
ruiz.signal: Prompt them to pick the three decisions they defend from the ones with a number attached that the board can check.
ruiz.misdirection: She'd lead with the best quarter, which tells the board which quarter to ask about.

osei.facts: Kessana and Straits Pacific will each have a line in the record, and the board reads the partners' lines. Standing with the Norwegian union is in the last quarter's results.
osei.stance: A company's partners write the part of the story it doesn't control.
osei.signal: Ask them what each of Halden's partners would say about them in one sentence, and whether that's in the defense.
osei.misdirection: He'd soften the account of Kessana, which the board has already read in the papers.

lund.facts: The board has read every memo. It will ask three things: did the decisions add up to a company; were they sound at the time; does the team understand its own run. The sentence the team wrote on its first day will be read aloud.
lund.stance: The board can forgive a wrong decision. It can't forgive not knowing which decisions were wrong.
lund.signal: Ask them to name the decision they'd most like the board not to ask about, and to put it in the defense first.
lund.misdirection: She'd have them write the defense as a strategy paper about the energy transition, which is her question, not the board's.

priya.facts: Erik wants the case in writing by the end of the quarter. Margrethe has read everything. Grant has the numbers and will ask about the quarter the team's score fell most. Marcus has been asked to speak for five minutes and hasn't said what about. Ingrid has been asked whether the job should exist, and has said she'll answer in the meeting.
priya.stance: Predictions: Grant asks about your worst quarter in the first ten minutes. Marcus speaks about Baton Rouge and the crude price, whatever you set it to. Margrethe asks about the sentence last, and means it. Ingrid backs the job if the defense gives her a reason she can repeat.
priya.misdirection: She thinks the board has made up its mind. It has made up half of it.
